label: Docs Analyser, now on its own
title: Can AI agents *use your docs?*
body: Paste a documentation portal and get a 0 to 100 score for how well agents find, read and use it.
captions:
The Docs Analyser is now a standalone tool.

Paste the URL of a documentation portal and it scores, from 0 to 100, how well AI agents can find, read and use it. It runs 27 checks in five groups, from API discovery to bot policy, and tells you what failed, why it matters and how to fix it.

No account, no migration, no spec upload. It reads the docs you already publish.

doctorine.dev

Coding agents now read your API docs before most developers do. The question is whether they get anything useful out of them.

The Docs Analyser answers that for any public portal: a 0 to 100 score, five category scores and a check list with the fix for each miss. It is free and it works on the docs you already have.

doctorine.dev

We have split the Docs Analyser out into its own tool.

One input, your docs URL. One output, a report on whether agents can discover your API, read your pages as Markdown, find what changed and reach the content without hitting a wall.

Run it on your own portal and see what an agent sees.

doctorine.dev

label: doctorine.dev
title: One URL in. What an agent sees, out.
captions:
Paste your docs URL, press Analyze, and read the report.

The analyser checks whether agents can discover your API, read your pages as Markdown, tell fresh pages from stale ones and reach the content without a challenge wall. Every miss comes with why it matters and how to fix it.

doctorine.dev

The fastest way to know how agents experience your documentation is to look at it the way they do.

That is what the Docs Analyser does: one URL, 27 checks, a score out of 100 and a report you can share with the team that owns the portal.

doctorine.dev

Before you write an llms.txt or ship an MCP server, find out what is already there.

The Docs Analyser reads your public portal and tells you which agent-facing pieces exist, which are missing and which could not be verified. It takes about ten seconds.

doctorine.dev

angle: We ran it on 33 docs sites
label: Docs Analyser, 25 September 2026
title: Public API docs sites, one analyser, one day. Here is what we saw.
captions:
We ran the Docs Analyser on 33 well-known public API documentation sites on 25 September 2026, from payments and messaging to developer platforms and AI labs.

16 returned a full score, between 52 and 95 with a median of 74. The other 17 came back as incomplete scans, which we report as such rather than guess. Over the next posts we share what the results have in common.

doctorine.dev

33 API docs sites, one tool, one day.

The short version: almost every site is readable by agents, and very few tell agents where the API is. 27 of the 33 had no API Catalog and 27 had no MCP Server Card. Every site where the check could run served its content without needing JavaScript.

The full run log is public, and you can run the same check on your own docs.

doctorine.dev

We wanted to know what agent-ready API docs look like in practice, so we ran our own analyser on 33 of the best-known public portals.

What we found is less about good and bad docs and more about which layer is missing. The pages are fine. The machine-readable signposts around them mostly are not there yet.

doctorine.dev

label: 16 full scores
title: The range across the API docs sites that returned a full score. *Median 74.*
captions:
Of the 33 API docs sites we ran through the Docs Analyser, 16 returned a full score. The lowest was 52, the highest 95, and the median 74.

Six scored 87 or more and were labelled agent-ready. The analyser does not grade the writing; what separated the top from the bottom was whether an agent could ask for Markdown and find the API from a standard location.

doctorine.dev

52 to 95.

That is the spread across 16 well-known API docs portals on 25 September 2026. None of them is badly written. The difference is in the plumbing agents rely on: content negotiation, catalogs, discovery links and fresh sitemaps.

The good news is that most of it is a configuration change, not a rewrite.

doctorine.dev

A 43-point gap between well-known API docs sites, measured the same way on the same day.

The median was 74 and six sites scored 87 or more. The lower half shared a pattern we will cover next: agents asking for Markdown got HTML back.

doctorine.dev

label: Most common miss
title: API docs sites with no API Catalog. The same number had no MCP Server Card.
captions:
The most common miss in our run of 33 API docs sites was not about content at all.

27 had no API Catalog, the well-known file that points agents to the API descriptions a company publishes. 27 had no MCP Server Card, the file that tells an agent which MCP server exists and how to connect before it opens a session.

Both are small files. Without them, an agent has to guess from prose and navigation.

doctorine.dev

27 of 33.

That is how many well-known API docs sites had no machine-readable catalog of their APIs when we ran the Docs Analyser on 25 September 2026. The same number had no MCP Server Card.

Agents are good at reading pages. They are much better when you tell them where the contract is.

doctorine.dev

If you fix one thing after running the Docs Analyser, it is probably discovery.

Across 33 public API docs sites, API Catalog and MCP Server Card were each missing on 27. These checks come from the Cloudflare Agent Ready benchmark, which the analyser runs alongside its own probes, so they were measured on every site.

doctorine.dev

label: Category scores
title: Agents can read most docs. *They struggle to find the API.*
body: Average across 16 scored sites: discovery 40, findability 83, delivery 91.
captions:
Every report breaks the score into five groups: agent and API discovery, findability, delivery and efficiency, readable content, and bot policy and trust.

Across the 16 API docs sites that returned a full score, discovery averaged 40. Findability averaged 83, and delivery and bot policy 91 each. Every site where the check could run served its docs without needing JavaScript.

The pages are there. The signposts to the API mostly are not.

doctorine.dev

The weakest group in our run was not content, speed or bot policy. It was discovery.

Agent and API discovery asks whether an agent can find the API catalog, the spec, the MCP server and the skills without reading the site like a human. Across 16 scored sites it averaged 40 out of 100.

doctorine.dev

Discovery 40. Findability 83. Delivery 91. Bot policy 91.

Those are the average category scores across 16 well-known API docs sites on 25 September 2026. Most teams have solved serving pages to agents. Far fewer have published the machine-readable map that tells an agent what the API is and where to start.

doctorine.dev

label: What separated the scores
title: Every site under 70 failed one check: *Markdown for agents.*
body: All nine sites at 73 or above passed it.
captions:
One check split our results cleanly.

Of the 16 API docs sites that returned a full score, all seven below 70 failed Markdown for agents: when an agent asks for Markdown, the site sends HTML. All nine at 73 or above passed it.

Markdown strips layout, cuts tokens and keeps the hierarchy an agent needs. It is also one of the easier fixes on the list.

doctorine.dev

If your docs score is in the fifties or sixties, check this first.

In our run of API docs sites, every site under 70 failed the same check, Markdown for agents, and every site at 73 or above passed it. The fix is to return a Markdown version of the page at the same URL, or to advertise one, when an agent asks for it.

doctorine.dev

Nine sites passed Markdown for agents and scored 73 or more. Seven failed it and scored under 70.

Correlation, not proof, and the sample is 16 sites. But it matches what Mintlify reports: by August 2026, 83% of agent traffic on its hosted docs used machine-friendly routes such as Markdown, llms.txt and skills.

doctorine.dev

label: Sitemap freshness
title: Docs sitemaps with no lastmod dates. Agents cannot tell current pages from abandoned ones.
captions:
A small check that surprised us: sitemap freshness.

12 of the 33 API docs sites we ran had a sitemap with no lastmod dates. That date is the one freshness signal a crawler can read without fetching every page. Without it, an agent either re-reads everything or cannot tell a current guide from one nobody has touched in years.

doctorine.dev

Your sitemap can tell agents which pages are current. On 12 of 33 API docs sites we checked, it did not.

The fix is to emit an accurate lastmod for every page from your docs build. Accurate matters: a date that changes on every deploy is as unhelpful as no date at all.

doctorine.dev

Developers complain about stale docs more than almost anything else. Agents have the same problem, and they do not complain.

On 12 of 33 docs sites in our run, the sitemap gave agents no way to judge freshness at all. The Docs Analyser flags it under findability, with the fix.

doctorine.dev

label: Top of the run
title: What a *95* looks like.
captions:
The highest score in our run was Resend at 95, followed by Notion at 93, Cloudflare and Clerk at 92, bunq at 91 and Vercel at 87.

What they share: Markdown at the same URL when an agent asks, a valid llms.txt, compact pages that do not waste tokens on chrome, and open bot policy. All six also scored above 50 on agent and API discovery, where the average across scored sites was 40.

doctorine.dev

Six API docs sites scored 87 or more in our run on 25 September 2026: Resend, Notion, Cloudflare, Clerk, bunq and Vercel.

None of them got there with better prose. They got there by answering agents in the format agents ask for and publishing the files agents look for first.

doctorine.dev

What does a 95 look like?

On Resend's docs on 25 September 2026, discovery, readable content, delivery and bot policy all scored 100. The only failed check was a redirect on the way to the content, plus one item flagged for review. It is a useful reference for anyone deciding what to fix first.

doctorine.dev

label: Reading a report
title: Strong pages. *Missing signposts.*
captions:
How to read a Docs Analyser report, using Stripe's docs as measured on 25 September 2026.

The score was 76, a strong foundation. Readable content and bot policy scored 100: agents get compact Markdown and are let in. The misses were all in discovery: no API catalog, no MCP server card, no working MCP endpoint on the docs origin, no agent discovery links, and a spec published as a GitHub repository rather than a fetchable document.

That is the typical shape: great pages, missing signposts.

doctorine.dev

The headline of every report is written the same way: the grade, then how many things agents looked for and did not find, each linked to its check.

For Stripe's docs on 25 September 2026 that was 76 and five things, all in agent and API discovery. Everything about reading the pages passed.

doctorine.dev

A score is only useful if it tells you what to do next.

Each report lists what was not found, what needs review and what could not be verified, and every miss opens into why it matters and how to fix it. You can share the report or send it by email to whoever owns the portal.

doctorine.dev

label: Mintlify, July 2026
title: Share of documentation traffic that came from AI agents on Mintlify-hosted docs.
captions:
Agents are now the main reader of API documentation.

On Mintlify-hosted docs, agents went from 15.2% of traffic at the start of 2026 to 66% in July, and roughly two agent requests for every human page load in August. In March, Claude Code and Cursor made up 95.6% of the agent traffic Mintlify could identify.

Sources: Mintlify, The state of agent traffic in documentation (March 2026), The state of docs traffic (July 2026) and State of Knowledge highlights (September 2026).

doctorine.dev

Two out of three.

That is the share of docs traffic Mintlify attributed to AI agents in July 2026, up from 15.2% at the start of the year. If your docs were designed for people clicking through a sidebar, most of your readers are now doing something else.

Source: Mintlify, The state of docs traffic, 29 July 2026.

doctorine.dev

Your docs have a new majority reader, and it does not use your navigation.

Mintlify reported 213M agent requests against 105M human page loads in July 2026, and 83% of agent traffic using machine-friendly routes like Markdown, llms.txt and skills by August. The Docs Analyser checks whether those routes exist on your portal.

Sources: Mintlify, July and September 2026.

doctorine.dev

angle: Markdown and llms.txt cut dead ends
label: 404s per agent task
title: With Markdown and llms.txt, down from 2.23 when agents navigated HTML.
captions:
Format changes how often an agent gets lost.

In Mintlify's navigation benchmark, 2,400 tests over 20 sites, agents hit 2.23 404 errors per task on HTML, 1.42 on Markdown and 0.11 on Markdown plus llms.txt, using up to 60% fewer tokens.

Source: Mintlify, Highlights from the 2026 State of Knowledge Report, 16 September 2026.

doctorine.dev

From 2.23 dead ends per task to 0.11.

That is the difference Mintlify measured between agents navigating HTML docs and agents given Markdown and an llms.txt index. In our own run of 33 API docs sites, 26 published a valid llms.txt, but only 19 returned Markdown when asked.

Source: Mintlify, September 2026.

doctorine.dev

Every 404 an agent hits is a guess that went wrong, and a guess that cost tokens.

Mintlify's benchmark put the number at 2.23 per task on HTML and 0.11 with Markdown plus llms.txt. The Docs Analyser checks both, along with real 404s, so an agent never mistakes an error page for content.

Source: Mintlify, 16 September 2026.

doctorine.dev

angle: A score is not a finished task
label: MCP-Universe, August 2025
title: Share of real MCP tasks GPT-5 completed. *Readable is not the same as usable.*
captions:
A readiness score tells you whether agents can find and read your docs. It does not tell you whether they can finish the job.

In Salesforce AI Research's MCP-Universe benchmark, GPT-5 completed 43.7% of real-world tasks on MCP servers. In WAPIIBench, no open-source model solved more than 40% of web API integration tasks, with hallucinated endpoints and wrong arguments.

Sources: MCP-Universe, arXiv 2508.14704; WAPIIBench, arXiv 2509.20172.

doctorine.dev

Static checks are necessary. They are not sufficient.

A docs portal can pass every discovery and Markdown check and an agent can still pick the wrong endpoint. Benchmarks put real task success well under half: 43.7% for GPT-5 on real MCP servers in MCP-Universe.

That gap, between readable and usable, is the part we are working on next.

Source: arXiv 2508.14704, August 2025.

doctorine.dev

Static agent readiness scores are now free: Fern launched one in April 2026, Cloudflare days later, and ours is at doctorine.dev. What none of them publishes is whether an agent actually completed a task against the API.

The benchmarks say that is where things break: 43.7% task success for GPT-5 on real MCP servers. A score is where you start. Task success is what your users feel.

Source: MCP-Universe, arXiv 2508.14704.

doctorine.dev

label: What comes next
title: Can an agent read your docs? Next question: *can it finish the task?*
captions:
The Docs Analyser answers the first question: can an agent find and read your documentation.

The next question is harder and more useful: given your docs, your spec and your MCP server, can a coding agent complete a real task against your API, and does it still manage after your next release. That is the direction we are building towards.

doctorine.dev

Reading is the easy part for an agent. Choosing the right endpoint, passing the right arguments and handling the error it gets back is where integrations fail.

We are extending Doctorine from a static score to a task check: real tasks, run by agents, against your API, with a record of what passed.

doctorine.dev

A static score measures what is on the page. A task eval measures what happens when an agent uses it.

We built the first to start the conversation, and it is free at doctorine.dev. The second is what we think every API release will need once agents are the main integrators.

doctorine.dev

label: Postman State of the API, 2025
title: Of API teams name inconsistent or outdated documentation as a collaboration blocker, the most cited one.
captions:
Docs drift is the oldest problem in API documentation, and agents make it quieter.

In Postman's 2025 State of the API survey of more than 5,700 respondents, 93% of teams reported collaboration blockers, and the most cited, by 55%, was inconsistent or outdated documentation. A developer who hits a stale page files a ticket. An agent just answers anyway.

Source: Postman, 2025 State of the API Report.

doctorine.dev

More than half of API teams name inconsistent or outdated documentation as a collaboration blocker, the most cited one in Postman's 2025 survey.

When the reader is an agent, stale docs do not produce a complaint. They produce a plausible integration that calls a field that no longer exists. The only fix that scales is checking every release before it ships.

Source: Postman, 2025 State of the API Report.

doctorine.dev

The spec changes, the docs lag, the SDK lags further.

55% of API teams in Postman's 2025 survey named inconsistent or outdated documentation as a blocker, more than any other. Doctorine starts from one approved API contract and publishes docs, SDKs, CLI, MCP server and skills from it, so they move together.

Source: Postman, 2025 State of the API Report.

doctorine.dev

label: Doctorine
title: Check every output. *Publish only what passed.*
body: Docs, SDKs, CLI, MCP server and Agent Skills from one approved API contract.
captions:
Most API tooling generates. Very little of it checks.

Doctorine turns one approved OpenAPI contract into a docs portal, TypeScript, Python and Go SDKs, a CLI, an MCP server and Agent Skills, checks each output before release, and publishes only what passed. Everything around the API ships as one release.

doctorine.dev

A release gate for everything around your API.

When the contract changes, every surface that depends on it has to change too, and the risk is the one that did not. Doctorine checks each output against the contract before release and holds back anything that fails.

doctorine.dev

Generating an SDK is the easy half. Keeping it honest after the next change is the hard half.

That is why Doctorine is built around a check, not a generator: one approved contract in, every output verified, only what passed goes out.

doctorine.dev

label: How to fix one check
title: Add an API Catalog. One file, at a well-known path.
captions:
The most common miss in our run of 33 API docs sites, and one of the smallest to fix.

An API Catalog is a machine-readable file at /.well-known/api-catalog (RFC 9727) that lists the API descriptions you publish, with links to each OpenAPI document. An agent that lands on your domain can read it and go straight to the contract instead of guessing from prose.

Publish it, point each entry at a fetchable spec, and run the analyser again.

doctorine.dev

How to fix API Catalog not found, in three steps.

Publish your OpenAPI description at a stable, fetchable URL, not only as a repository. Serve a catalog at /.well-known/api-catalog that links to it. Re-run the Docs Analyser to confirm it validates and lists a usable description.

27 of 33 sites in our run had not done this yet.

doctorine.dev

Why this matters, in the analyser's own words: agents can discover contracts directly instead of guessing from prose or client-side navigation.

The API Catalog is a small well-known file, defined in RFC 9727, that tells them where those contracts are. It is also the check most API docs sites in our run were missing.

doctorine.dev

label: Behind the checks
title: 27 checks, five groups, *and a fix for every miss.*
captions:
What the Docs Analyser actually does when you paste a URL.

It runs the Cloudflare Agent Ready benchmark and adds its own probes: whether missing pages return real 404s, whether URLs resolve without redirect chains, whether the sitemap carries dates, whether pages are readable without JavaScript, how many tokens a page costs, and whether an MCP endpoint answers a real initialize call.

Every check says what was assessed, why it matters and how to fix it.

doctorine.dev

27 checks in five groups: agent and API discovery, findability, delivery and efficiency, readable content, and bot policy and trust.

Some come from Cloudflare's Agent Ready benchmark. The rest are Doctorine's own probes, such as whether a missing page returns a real 404 instead of a page that looks like content, and whether the sitemap carries dates.

doctorine.dev

We do not just check whether an MCP server is declared. The analyser sends a real initialize request to the common MCP paths on your docs origin and reports whether anything answers.

The same idea runs through the other checks: test what an agent would do, not only what a file claims.

doctorine.dev

angle: No score beats a wrong score
label: Incomplete scans
title: Sites where the analyser could not verify enough signals, and said so instead of guessing.
captions:
An honest number from our run: 17 of the 33 API docs sites we tried came back as incomplete scans, even after retries.

When the analyser cannot verify enough of the signals, most often the API spec and MCP probes, it withholds the overall score and marks each check it could not verify. We would rather show you no number than a confident wrong one.

doctorine.dev

Not every scan finishes, and the report says so.

In our run of 33 docs sites, 17 returned Incomplete scan. The checks that could run are still listed as passed or missing, and the rest are marked unverified rather than counted as failures.

If your portal comes back incomplete, run it again later.

doctorine.dev

A tool that grades other people's docs should be strict with itself first.

The Docs Analyser only gives an overall score when enough of its 27 checks could be verified. On 25 September 2026 that was 16 of the 33 sites we ran. The other 17 got a partial report and no score.

doctorine.dev

angle: The spec is the weak link
label: APIs.guru, September 2026
title: Of the OpenAPI specs in the largest open directory are invalid. *Agents start from the spec.*
captions:
Everything an agent does against your API starts from the contract, and the contract is often the weakest part.

In the APIs.guru directory, 688 of 3,992 OpenAPI specs are invalid, 17.2%. In our own run of 33 docs sites, the analyser could confirm a fetchable machine-readable spec on 12; on 14 it could not verify either way.

Source: APIs.guru metrics API, queried 25 September 2026.

doctorine.dev

688 invalid specs out of 3,992.

That is the state of the largest open directory of OpenAPI definitions. A docs portal can be beautifully written and still hand agents a contract they cannot load. The analyser checks whether your spec is published, fetchable and affordable to ingest.

Source: APIs.guru, September 2026.

doctorine.dev

Before docs, before SDKs, before an MCP server, there is the spec.

17.2% of the specs in APIs.guru are invalid, and a published GitHub repository is not the same as a spec an agent can fetch. Doctorine starts every release from one approved contract for that reason.

Source: APIs.guru metrics API, 25 September 2026.

doctorine.dev
